claims.text: The initial magnetic high-entropy alloy is as-cast, single-phase, and homogeneous.
Moderate-temperature, timed annealing in an inert atmosphere can induce controlled nanoprecipitate formation in the alloy.
Appropriate annealing temperature and duration favor nanoscale precipitate nucleation without unwanted phase coarsening.
The proposed effect requires alloy compositions that permit nanoprecipitate formation.
Annealing-induced nanoscale precipitates act as magnetic domain-wall pinning centers.
Nanoprecipitate formation increases the density of domain-wall pinning sites.
An increased density of pinning sites hinders magnetic domain-wall motion.
Hindered domain-wall motion requires a higher external magnetic field to reverse magnetization.
The higher field required for magnetization reversal increases coercivity.
The annealed alloy will have a higher coercive field than an identically composed as-cast sample.
Significant precipitate coarsening or phase separation may prevent the predicted coercivity increase.
The magnitude of the coercive-field increase depends on annealing parameters and alloy composition.
Nanoprecipitate formation and distribution will be assessed using TEM and/or XRD.
Coercivity in treated and untreated samples will be measured using vibrating sample magnetometry.
Failure of the annealed samples to show a statistically significant coercivity increase, or failure to correlate nanoprecipitates with enhanced coercivity, would falsify the hypothesis.
